'''''Tuberaria guttata''''', the '''spotted rock-rose''' or '''annual rock-rose''', is an annual plant of the [[Mediterranean region]] which also occurs very locally in [[Wales]] and [[Ireland]]. The flowers are very variable with the characteristic spot at the base of the petal very variable in size and intensity of colour.

==Description==
''Tuberaria guttata'' is an [[annual plant]] that grows to {{convert|2|-|30|cm|0}} tall.<ref name="Proctor_1960">{{cite journal |author=M. C. F. Proctor |year=1960 |title=''Tuberaria guttata'' (L.) Fourreau |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=243–253 |jstor=2257323|doi=10.2307/2257323 }}</ref> It has a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] of basal leaves, each up to {{convert|3|cm|1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|cm|1|abbr=on}} wide, but this rosette has normally withered by the time the plant is in flower. The stems bear 2–5 opposite pairs of leaves, and a few smaller leaves higher up, arranged alternately.<ref name="Proctor_1960"/>

The [[inflorescence]] comprises around 12 flowers, {{convert|8|-|12|mm|abbr=on}} in diameter. Each flower has five uneven sepals and five yellow petals usually with a dark red spot near the base.<ref name="Proctor_1960"/> The flowers are [[cleistogamy|cleistogamous]],<ref name="Jepson"/> producing little [[pollen]] and no [[nectar]], and attracting few insect visitors,<ref name="Herrera">{{cite journal |author=Javier Herrera |year=2004 |title=Lifetime fecundity and floral variation in ''Tuberaria guttata'' (Cistaceae), a Mediterranean annual |journal=[[Plant Ecology]] |volume=172 |issue=2 |pages=219–225 |doi=10.1023/B:VEGE.0000026340.53858.44|s2cid=22458599 }}</ref> and the petals fall off after only a few hours.<ref name="Proctor_1960"/> The centre of the flower houses around 20 [[stamen]]s and a single capitate [[stigma (botany)|stigma]].<ref name="Proctor_1960"/>

The [[fruit]] of ''T. guttata'' is a [[capsule (botany)|capsule]] containing many seeds, each {{convert|0.6|mm}} long.<ref name="Proctor_1960"/>

==Distribution and ecology==
''Tuberaria guttata'' is widely distributed in the Mediterranean region, and has a continuous distribution along the French Atlantic coast as far as the [[Channel Islands]].<ref name="Proctor_1962"/> Further north, its distribution is very patchy, being confined to a few localities on the west coasts of Ireland and Wales.<ref name="Proctor_1962"/> The best-known of these populations is on the slopes of [[Holyhead Mountain]] in [[Anglesey]].<ref name="Proctor_1962"/> These British populations mark the northernmost limit of the species' distribution.<ref name="Proctor_1962"/> ''Tuberaria guttata'' was chosen by [[Plantlife]] as the [[County flowers of the United Kingdom|county flower]] of Anglesey in 2002.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/plant_species/spotted_rock-rose/ |publisher=[[Plantlife]] |title=Spotted rock-rose, (''Tuberaria guttata'') |access-date=17 April 2015}}</ref>

In [[California]], ''T. guttata'' has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in the foothills of the [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]] on the eastern edge of the [[Sacramento Valley]].<ref name="Jepson">{{cite web |url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=47425 |title=''T. guttata'' (L.) Fourr. |publisher=[[Jepson Herbarium]], [[University of California, Berkeley]] |access-date=17 April 2015}}</ref>

In the Mediterranean region, ''T. guttata'' is common in arid habitats from woodlands to grasslands and roadsides.<ref name="Herrera"/> In the British Isles, it grows "in bare patches of thin, dry soil overlying hard igneous rock in open areas within wind-cut heath near the sea".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=plant/tuberaria-guttata |title=''Tuberaria guttata'' (Spotted Rock-rose) |work=Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |publisher=[[Biological Records Centre]] |access-date=17 April 2015}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Tuberaria guttata'' was [[species description|first described]] by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as "''Cistus guttatus''" in his 1753 work ''{{lang|la|[[Species Plantarum]]}}''. It was transferred to the genus ''[[Tuberaria]]'' by [[Jules Pierre Fourreau]] in 1868.

The Welsh populations were described as a separate species in 1844 by [[Jules Émile Planchon]]. He named the plants "''Helianthemum breweri''", after [[Samuel Brewer]], who had discovered the population in 1726.<ref name="Proctor_1962">{{cite journal |author=M. C. F. Proctor |title=The British forms of ''Tuberaria guttata'' (L.) Fourreau |journal=[[Watsonia (journal)|Watsonia]] |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=236–250 |url=http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats5p236.pdf }}</ref> This is now considered a synonym of ''T. guttata''.<ref name="Proctor_1962"/>
